topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.notes:
Simple harmonic motion is any oscillation where the restoring force (and acceleration) is proportional to displacement and points back toward equilibrium: a = −ω²x. Everything else in this topic follows from that one relationship.

The velocity at any displacement x, given amplitude A, is v = ω√(A²−x²) — maximum at the center (x=0, where v_max = ωA) and zero at the extremes (x=±A). This single formula answers most 'find velocity at this position' questions directly, without needing to know the time.

Angular frequency connects to ordinary frequency and period by ω = 2πf = 2π/T. A frequent exam pattern gives you a displacement equation like x = A sin(ωt+φ) directly — read ω straight off the coefficient of t, and A off the amplitude in front, rather than re-deriving them.

For a simple pendulum specifically, T = 2π√(L/g) — critically, this does NOT depend on mass or amplitude (for small swings). Any question about 'what happens if you double the mass' has the same answer: nothing. Only length (and gravity) matter.

KEY FORMULA: v = ω√(A² − x²).

topics.title: Waves & Sound
topics.notes:
A wave on a string travels at speed v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is the linear mass density (mass per unit length). This single formula is behind almost every 'wire/rope/wave speed' question in past papers — the only real work is correctly computing μ = mass/length from whatever's given.

For a string or pipe producing a standing wave, the fundamental frequency depends on the wave speed and the effective length: for a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe open at both ends), f = v/(2L); for a pipe closed at one end, f = v/(4L). 'Effective length' sometimes needs a small end correction added for pipes, since the antinode doesn't form exactly at the physical opening — past questions occasionally give you this correction directly.

Beats occur when two sounds of slightly different frequency interfere, producing a periodic rise and fall in loudness. The beat frequency is simply the difference between the two source frequencies: f_beat = |f₁−f₂|.

The Doppler effect changes the frequency you hear based on relative motion between source and observer. The general form is f' = f×(v±v_observer)/(v∓v_source) — the key skill is getting the signs right: use + in the numerator when the observer moves toward the source, − when moving away; use − in the denominator when the source moves toward the observer, + when moving away. Drawing a quick diagram of who's moving which direction before plugging in numbers avoids almost all sign errors here.

KEY FORMULA: v = √(T/μ) for wave speed on a string; f' = f(v±v_o)/(v∓v_s) for Doppler shift.

topics.title: Optics — Mirrors
topics.notes:
Curved mirrors form images according to the mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where u is object distance, v is image distance, and f is focal length (f = R/2, half the radius of curvature). Sign conventions matter enormously here — this is where most mistakes happen. A common working convention: distances measured in the direction light actually travels are positive, so a real image (in front of the mirror) is positive, while a virtual image (behind the mirror) comes out negative.

Whether an image is virtual or real, erect or inverted, magnified or diminished depends entirely on where the object sits relative to the focal point. For a concave mirror specifically: an object beyond the center of curvature gives a real, inverted, diminished image; between the focal point and center of curvature gives real, inverted, magnified; and — this is the case tested repeatedly in past papers — an object INSIDE the focal length gives a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror. That last case is what a shaving or makeup mirror does.

Magnification is m = −v/u. The sign tells you orientation (negative means inverted, positive means erect), and the magnitude tells you how much bigger or smaller the image is compared to the object.

KEY FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, and magnification m = −v/u.

topics.title: Damped Oscillations & Resonance
topics.notes:
Real oscillating systems lose energy over time to friction or resistance — this is damping. How a system responds depends on how strong that damping is, and there are three named cases worth knowing cold for concept questions: underdamped (the system oscillates, but with steadily shrinking amplitude, like a guitar string ringing out), critically damped (the system returns to equilibrium as fast as possible with no oscillation at all — this is what well-designed shock absorbers or door closers aim for), and overdamped (the system returns to equilibrium without oscillating, but more slowly and sluggishly than the critical case).

Resonance is what happens when an external driving force pushes a system at exactly its natural oscillation frequency. Because the pushes arrive perfectly in sync with the system's own rhythm, energy builds up efficiently and amplitude grows dramatically — sometimes destructively, which is why bridges and buildings are engineered to avoid matching common driving frequencies (wind, footsteps, engines).

The distinction that trips students up: damping and resonance are almost opposite concerns. Damping is about a system losing energy and settling down; resonance is about a system gaining energy efficiently from a well-timed external push. A 'why does this bridge sway violently' question is a resonance question; a 'why does this car not bounce after hitting a bump' question is a damping question.

KEY IDEA: Resonance occurs when driving frequency = natural frequency; critically damped systems return to equilibrium fastest without oscillating.
